passage: Bilal's final design portfolio for his course in Berlin had been ninety percent finished since March. Twelve projects, all laid out. Only the captions, a cover page and the upload to the school portal remained. It was now May. Every Sunday he opened the file, changed a font, then closed it. His flatmate Astrid finally asked, "What's actually left?" He listed it: two hours of work, maybe three. "So why not tonight?" Bilal went quiet. "Because then the tutors will see it. Right now it's still good in my head." Astrid nodded slowly. "Upload it by Friday, and I'll buy the pizza." He wrote the captions that night, hands a little cold.

qa.q: How many projects were in Bilal's portfolio?
qa.a: There were twelve projects.

qa.q: What was Bilal really afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid of the tutors judging it; while unsubmitted, it stayed good in his head, so avoiding the last steps protected him from that fear.

qa.q: What helped Bilal finally act, and why?
qa.a: Astrid asked what was actually left and set a Friday deadline with a small reward, which made the last two or three hours concrete and shared.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Bilal's weekly font-changing?
qa.a: Astrid seems to see through it gently, guessing it is not laziness, and offers support instead of teasing.

grounding: Shows a student leaving the final polish and submission undone for weeks because finishing means being judged.

passage: The electronics lab at the engineering college was almost empty in the vacation. Karthik sat by the soldering bench with his final-year project report, a smart irrigation sensor. The circuit worked. The report was written. What remained was the formatting, the references and his guide's signature. That had been true for five weeks. Disha, the lab assistant, looked over. "Still here, Karthik? I thought you submitted in June." He laughed awkwardly. "Just checking the graphs again." Disha set down her tray. "Checking or hiding?" His smile faded. "What if Sir reads it and says it's weak?" "Then he'll say it, and you'll fix it. Right now it can't even be weak." Karthik opened the references page.

qa.q: What was Karthik's final-year project?
qa.a: It was a smart irrigation sensor.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when Disha asked, "Checking or hiding?"
qa.a: He felt exposed and anxious, afraid that his guide would call the report weak.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik to do next?
qa.a: Finish the formatting and references in one sitting and take the report for the guide's signature, accepting that any criticism can be fixed.

qa.q: How does Disha see Karthik's five weeks of checking?
qa.a: Disha sees it as avoidance rather than care, and nudges him kindly with a direct question.

grounding: A student leaves the last formatting and submission undone for weeks, and a lab assistant sees the fear underneath.

passage:
Dear Yusuf sir,

I owe you an honest update. The short film you mentored me on is done except the colour correction, the credits and the festival form. It has been that way since the first week of August.

I told myself I was busy. The truth is I've watched it thirty times and each time I'm more scared. Once I send it, the jury will decide if it's any good. Right now I can still believe it is.

I have booked the editing room for Saturday. If I can finish the credits there, I'll submit on Sunday night. Could I send you the link before I do?

Thank you for not giving up on me,
Damini

qa.q: What three things were left on Damini's film?
qa.a: The colour correction, the credits and the festival form were left.

qa.q: How does Damini feel each time the film is watched again?
qa.a: Damini feels more scared each time, afraid of the jury deciding the film is not good.

qa.q: Which step in the letter makes finishing more likely?
qa.a: Booking the editing room for Saturday and naming Sunday night for submission turn a vague intention into a fixed plan.

qa.q: How might Yusuf sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Yusuf sir is likely relieved and touched by Damini's honesty, and glad to see the film before it goes out.

grounding: A student admits in a letter to leaving the final polish and submission undone for weeks out of fear of being judged.

passage: In the college hostel near Ahmednagar, Chinmay's field project on groundwater had dragged for three months the year before. This semester, before collecting a single sample, he tore a page from his notebook and wrote: "DONE means: 20 well readings taken, table typed, two-page report printed, signed by Nandini ma'am, one copy given to the gram panchayat office." He pinned it above his bed. In week six, the report was typed and he felt the old urge to keep tweaking the graphs. He looked at the page. Graphs weren't on it. He printed, got the signature and took the bus to the panchayat. At the office, he ticked the last line.

qa.q: How many well readings did Chinmay's list include?
qa.a: His list included 20 well readings.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in week six when he wanted to tweak the graphs?
qa.a: He felt the old pull to keep polishing, a mix of habit and uncertainty about whether the report was good enough.

qa.q: Why did the written list help Chinmay stop?
qa.a: It set a clear endpoint in advance, so when he wanted to tweak graphs he could check that they were not part of done and move on.

qa.q: How might Nandini ma'am see Chinmay's project this time?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased and a little surprised to see him finish on time, after last year's project dragged for months.

grounding: Shows a student writing down in advance exactly what finished means so the project ends by decision, not drift.

passage: Clara had one rule for her statistics essays at university in Uppsala: before opening the data, she wrote a sticky note that said what done meant. For this one: "2,000 words. Three charts. Checked once for typos. Uploaded to the course site by Thursday, 5 p.m." Her friend Ingrid laughed at the note. "You're so strict." "Last year I had an essay at ninety-five percent for a month," Clara said. "It was never really done, just abandoned." On Thursday at three, Clara reached the typo check. She wanted to rewrite the conclusion again. She looked at the note, sighed, uploaded, and felt a surprising lightness walking to the café.

qa.q: When did Clara's note say the essay had to be uploaded?
qa.a: By Thursday, 5 p.m.

qa.q: What did Clara feel after uploading the essay?
qa.a: She felt a surprising lightness, relieved that stopping had been her decision instead of a drift.

qa.q: What could Ingrid borrow from Clara's method?
qa.a: Ingrid could write a clear definition of done before starting, with word count, checks and upload time, so there is no endless ninety-five percent.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see Clara's sticky note at first?
qa.a: Ingrid finds it funny and a bit strict, not knowing about the essay that sat at ninety-five percent for a month.

grounding: Shows a student writing what finished looks like before starting, so stopping becomes a clear decision.

passage: The college canteen committee met in a small room behind the kitchen. Mridul, a second-year student, had volunteered to run the survey on new menu items. Minakshi, the committee secretary, remembered last year's survey that never really ended. "What does finished look like?" she asked. Mridul thought, then wrote on the whiteboard: "Form shared with all hostels. 300 responses or Friday noon, whichever first. Results chart made. Presented at Monday meeting." She nodded. On Friday the count was 284. He wanted to wait for more. He looked at the board, closed the form at noon, and presented on Monday. The new lemon rice was on the menu by Wednesday.

qa.q: How many responses had come in by Friday?
qa.a: The count was 284.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when the count was 284?
qa.a: He felt tempted and uncertain, wanting to wait for more responses to reach the number.

qa.a: Writing an endpoint of 300 responses or Friday noon made closing the form a clear decision, so the results reached the menu quickly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel about this survey compared to last year's?
qa.a: Minakshi likely feels relieved and pleased, since this one had a clear end and led to a real menu change.

grounding: A student defines finished in advance on a whiteboard, turning the survey's end into a decision rather than a drift.

subtype: Colleague who starts but does not close [Receiver]
passage: I'm Pooja, and for a year I sat next to Damini at the marketing agency. Damini is brilliant at starts. She'd pitch an idea on Monday, draft half the slides by Tuesday and then be onto something new. The loose ends came to me. I'd find her half-written client email in the shared folder at six and finish it. I'd chase the printer for the brochure she'd ordered and forgotten. Nobody noticed. Our manager praised Damini's energy at the review. I went home and cried in the auto, tired and invisible. The next week I made a shared tracker with an owner for every task, including hers. It helped, a little.

qa.a: Pooja found a half-written client email.

subtype: Colleague who starts but does not close [Receiver]
passage:
Supervisor's note, IT support desk, end of quarter.
I've noticed a pattern I should have caught sooner. Divyansh opens tickets quickly and gives users a cheerful first reply. But many of his tickets stay half-resolved, and Gautam has been closing them, often after hours. This month Gautam closed fourteen tickets that Divyansh had opened. When I asked Gautam about it, he looked at the floor and said, "Someone has to." He sounded worn out, not proud. Divyansh seemed genuinely surprised when I showed him the list. Next step: from Monday, every ticket stays with the person who opens it until closed, and I'll check the list each Friday.

qa.q: How many tickets did Gautam close that Divyansh had opened?
qa.a: Gautam closed fourteen tickets that Divyansh had opened.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he said, "Someone has to"?
qa.a: He felt worn out and quietly resentful, looking at the floor rather than sounding proud.

qa.q: What change did the supervisor make, and how could it help?
qa.a: Every ticket now stays with whoever opens it until closed, with a Friday check, so the hidden work stops falling on Gautam.

qa.q: How did Divyansh react when shown the list?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed genuinely surprised, since the cost of his half-finished tickets had been invisible to him.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows how one colleague quietly finishes another's loose ends, and the cost of that invisible work.

subtype: Colleague who starts but does not close [Receiver]
passage:
Tuesday night.
Did Nilesh's work again today. He started the vendor comparison sheet last week, very excited, filled in three suppliers and then left for a conference. Our manager asked for it at four. I finished the other five suppliers by seven. Nilesh texted "thanks yaar, you're a lifesaver 😊" and that was it.
I'm not angry at him exactly. He means well. But this is the fourth time this month, and I'm the one missing dinner. I feel used, and a bit stupid for not saying anything.
Tomorrow I'm going to tell him, calmly, that he needs to close what he opens, or hand it over properly.
Shalini

qa.q: How many suppliers had Nilesh filled in?
qa.a: He filled in three suppliers.

qa.q: What is Shalini feeling after finishing the sheet?
qa.a: Shalini feels used and a bit stupid for staying quiet, though not exactly angry at Nilesh.

qa.q: What does Shalini plan to say, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: To tell Nilesh calmly that he must close what he opens or hand it over properly, which names the problem without an attack.

qa.q: How does Nilesh seem to see the situation?
qa.a: Nilesh seems grateful but unaware, sending a cheerful thanks without noticing that this is the fourth time Shalini has covered.

grounding: A worker's diary records the hidden cost of repeatedly finishing a colleague's half-done tasks.

passage: Keerthana had started a small tailoring unit in her family's front room in Palani, stitching cloth shopping bags. For two months she had been perfecting the first batch: redoing handles, changing the fabric, re-cutting pockets. Her cousin Shreya, who ran a provision store, finally said, "Give me twenty. Whatever state they're in. Let customers decide." Keerthana's stomach turned. Two bags had slightly uneven seams. She delivered all twenty anyway, with a notebook for comments. In a week, fourteen had sold. Customers wrote that they wanted a longer strap and a zip. Nobody wrote about the seams. Keerthana bought zips on Monday and started the second batch, lighter than she'd felt in months.

qa.q: How many bags did Keerthana deliver to Shreya?
qa.a: She delivered all twenty.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she handed over bags with uneven seams?
qa.a: Her stomach turned; she felt nervous and exposed, worried the imperfect seams would be judged.

qa.q: What did the good-enough batch teach Keerthana that months of perfecting did not?
qa.a: Real customers wanted a longer strap and a zip, feedback she only got by letting the imperfect bags leave the room.

qa.q: How does Shreya see the two months of perfecting?
qa.a: Shreya seems to see it as holding back for no reason, and pushes her cousin to let customers decide.

grounding: Shows a young worker releasing a good-enough first batch, getting feedback and improving instead of chasing perfection.

passage: Alejandro, in his second year teaching Spanish at a secondary school in Seville, had been building a set of grammar worksheets for weeks. He wanted every page perfect: the right pictures, no mistakes, clever examples. His colleague Astrid watched him redo page four for the third time. "Just give them to one class tomorrow," she said. "See where they get stuck." He winced, but he printed ten pages that night, typos included. The next day, a student pointed out a mistake in exercise six. Three students were confused by the instructions on page two. Alejandro rewrote those two things that evening. By Friday version two went to all his classes.

qa.q: Which exercise had a mistake in it?
qa.a: A student pointed out a mistake in exercise six.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when Astrid suggested using the worksheets tomorrow?
qa.a: He winced, feeling uneasy and exposed at the thought of showing imperfect pages to students.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Using a good-enough version with one class quickly showed the real problems in exercise six and page two, which weeks of polishing had not found.

qa.q: How might the students be affected by version two?
qa.a: They get clearer instructions and correct exercises, shaped by the problems they themselves pointed out.

grounding: Illustrates a worker using an imperfect version, gathering feedback and improving it instead of holding out for perfection.

subtype: Attention pulled by whatever is nearby [Actor]
passage: In the Mumbai flat, Ritu sat on the floor to put on her school shoes. Her big sister Sarita was waiting at the door with the bag. Ritu pushed her left foot into one shoe. Then she saw her toy bus under the sofa. She pulled it out and rolled it along the tiles. "Vroom." She drove it to the kitchen and back. The second shoe lay forgotten by the door. "Ritu! Shoes!" Sarita called. Ritu looked down, surprised to see one bare foot. Sarita put the bus on the shelf and held out the shoe.

passage: The after-school study room at the hostel had one television, mounted high in the corner, and today it showed a cricket match. Mohit, eleven, had fifteen maths sums. He sat at the table nearest the TV. He solved one, looked up at the screen. Solved another. A boundary was hit; everyone cheered, and Mohit forgot what seven times eight was. By dinner he had done eight sums. Naveen sir, the warden, noticed. "Mohit, tomorrow sit at the back table, facing the wall." The next evening Mohit finished all fifteen in forty minutes and was surprised that it had been so quick.

passage:
Monday. Chaitanya, ten, did his English homework on the sofa while his mother Seema's phone played videos next to him. Every few minutes he glanced over. Two pages of writing took him an hour and a half.
Wednesday. Seema noticed and put the phone in her bedroom while he worked at the dining table. He grumbled. "I wasn't even watching." Still, he finished in forty-five minutes.
Saturday. Chaitanya set up the table himself, without being asked, and asked her to take the phone to her room. "It's quicker," he said. He finished his worksheet and went out to play before lunch, looking pleased.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya do his homework on Monday?
qa.a: He did his English homework on the sofa.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya grumble on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt a little defensive and annoyed, insisting he wasn't even watching, not yet seeing how the phone slowed him.

qa.a: Moving the phone to the bedroom and working at the dining table removed the screen's pull, halving his homework time.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on Saturday?
qa.a: Seema would likely feel pleased and proud that Chaitanya set up the table himself and asked for the phone to be moved.

grounding: Shows across days a child whose homework takes twice as long with a screen nearby, and faster once it is moved away.

subtype: Homework with phone or TV near [Actor]
passage: Uma, beta, sit, I'll tell you about your father when he was nine. We had just got our first television, black and white. Hemant would do his homework on the floor right in front of it, and I'd hear, "Just one minute, Amma, just this song." Two pages of arithmetic took him all evening. I scolded, and it didn't help. He wasn't being naughty; the moving pictures simply pulled his eyes. One day his teacher sent a note home. That evening, I moved his books to the verandah, far from the TV, and sat with my knitting. He finished in half an hour and then ran to watch his programme, guilt-free.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and in Class 11 I did an experiment on myself. My friend Pallavi said I was always on my phone, and I laughed. "I just check it." So she made me note every time I picked it up during a Sunday of studying. I lost count at forty. Worse, one "quick look" at a video at two o'clock ended at three. I didn't remember choosing to keep watching; the next video just started. I felt sick, honestly, and a bit cheated. After that I switched off autoplay and kept the phone in my bag during study hours. It didn't make me perfect. It made stopping possible.

Imran arrived for evening practice and sat on the bench to change. He took out his phone "for one second". passage: In Jaya's village near Sirsi, the only good signal was on the roof, and the only quiet place was her grandmother's room. With board exams two months away, Jaya made a plan. She stopped scolding herself before bed, because there was nothing to scold.

passage: Mateo, sixteen, lived in a small flat in Buenos Aires with his sister Ada, who was studying for university entrance. Mateo was always behind; Ada never was. One night he asked her secret. He felt twitchy for twenty minutes, then forgot the drawer. He finished his chemistry questions by half past eight.

passage: Ganga, nineteen, studied for her BCom exams in her family's small house in Mandya. She liked to think she was efficient. Her phone played songs, a video lecture ran on the laptop, and her class group chat pinged every minute. She answered Sabina about the bus timings, typed notes, sang along, replied again. At ten she closed the laptop, satisfied: four hours of work. The next morning, Sabina quizzed her on the accounting chapter over tea. Ganga couldn't explain depreciation, which she had "studied" last night. Her face fell. That evening she tried one hour with only the book. She remembered more from that hour than from the four before.

passage: Yuki, twenty, had a history test at her university in Osaka. On Sunday afternoon she spread out her notes, opened a music playlist, kept a drama episode running in a small window "for background" and replied to Aiko's messages about a festival. On Monday, halfway through the test, she stared at a question about the treaty she had highlighted in bright yellow. Nothing came. Walking out, she told Aiko, "I was so busy. How did I learn nothing?" Aiko said, "You were busy switching." Yuki thought about that all the way home.

qa.a: She felt confused and frustrated, having felt busy all Sunday yet unable to recall the treaty.

passage: In the university library's group room, Urmila had three windows open: her economics notes, a chat with her project group and a comedy clip. Earphones played music. He slid his phone into his bag. "Try forty minutes, notes only. Then we'll check messages together." She groaned, but closed the chat. At the end, she explained elasticity in two sentences and felt a small, surprised pride. "Okay. That's annoying," she said, smiling.

passage: Devika, twenty-four, was the only engineer at the small water-board office in Karad. That Tuesday she had to finish the pipeline pressure calculations before the district officer's visit.
